steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a medical imaging paper on detecting diabetic retinopathy severity changes with longitudinal self-supervised learning. Give the clinical background on DR and its grading, review deep learning, self-supervised and longitudinal approaches, and state what we do and evaluate.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Clinical background: diabetes, diabetic retinopathy, screening and grading
- Deep learning for DR grading and use of longitudinal information
- Self-supervised learning and contrastive methods
- Longitudinal self-supervised learning (LSSL) pretext tasks
- Our aim, methods and evaluation

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Clinical background
  - International Diabetes Federation: people with diabetes expected to reach 700 million by 2045
  - DR affects over one-third of them; leading cause of vision loss worldwide
  - mechanism: high blood sugar damages retinal blood vessels -> swelling, leakage; lesions in fundus images = leaking blood, fluids; red and bright lesions common in screening
  - early detection reduces blindness incidence
  - color fundus photographs (CFP) used clinically: microaneurysms, hemorrhages, soft/hard exudates
  - severity scale: no apparent DR, mild NPDR, moderate NPDR, severe NPDR, PDR = grades 0-4 (Fig. 1)
  - NPDR (1, 2, 3): early-to-middle stage, progressive microvascular disease, small vessel damage + occlusions
  - PDR (4): potential visual loss, often massive hemorrhage
  - early identification + treatment (mild to moderate NPDR) may slow progression, prevent impairment and blindness
- Deep learning for DR
  - great success in medical image analysis; supervised CNN methods for automated DR grading
  - rarely use longitudinal information
  - Yan et al.: Siamese network, different pre-training and fusion schemes, early stage DR from longitudinal CFP pairs of same patient
- Self-supervised learning
  - learns robust high-level representations via pretext tasks before supervised downstream task
  - current SSL mostly contrastive
  - choosing pretext task not straightforward; contrastive learning on medical images relatively limited
  - lesion-based contrastive learning for automated DR grading
- Longitudinal SSL
  - new pretext task for classification in longitudinal context
  - Rivail et al.: Siamese model predicts time interval between two consecutive longitudinal retinal OCT acquisitions -> disease progression
  - Zhao et al.: LSSL auto-encoder, two consecutive scans; reconstruction term + time alignment term (latent topology changes in direction of longitudinal change)
  - extension: dynamic graph per training batch defines neighborhood in latent space; connects nearby subjects, aligns progression directions -> smooth trajectory field
- Our work
  - LSSL to capture progression and predict change from no DR/mild NPDR (grade 0 or 1) to more severe DR (grade \geq 2) over two consecutive follow-ups
  - three methods using current + prior examinations
  - evaluation on OPHDIAT dataset
  - first to assess early DR severity changes between consecutive images with SSL in longitudinal context

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The International Diabetes Federation expects that the number of people affected by diabetes will reach 700 million by 2045. Diabetic retinopathy (DR) affects more than one-third of this population and it is the leading cause of vision loss worldwide. DR happens when high blood sugar levels damage the retinal blood vessels, which causes swelling and leakage. In fundus retina images the lesions appear as leaking blood and fluids. Red lesions and bright lesions are the types of lesions that are commonly identified during DR screening. If DR is detected at an early stage, the incidence of blindness can be reduced. In clinical routine, color fundus photographs (CFP) are used to identify morphological changes of the retina, by looking at the presence of retinal lesions like microaneurysms, hemorrhages, and soft or hard exudates. The international clinical DR severity scale has five levels: no apparent DR, mild non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR), moderate NPDR, severe NPDR, and proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), which are labeled as grades 0, 1, 2, 3 (shown in Fig. 1) and 4. NPDR (grades 1, 2, 3) is the early-to-middle stage of DR, and it is a progressive microvascular disease with small vessel damages and occlusions. PDR (grade 4) is the period of potential visual loss, which is often caused by a massive hemorrhage. Identifying DR early and treating it adequately, especially in the mild to moderate stage of NPDR, may slow down the progression of DR and so prevent diabetes-related visual impairments and blindness.

In the past years deep learning has been very successful in medical image analysis. Many supervised learning techniques based on convolutional neural networks have been proposed for the automated DR grading task. But these approaches rarely make use of longitudinal information. In this direction, Yan et al. proposed to use a Siamese network with different pre-training and fusion schemes to detect the early stage of DR with longitudinal pairs of CFP acquired from the same patient. Self-supervised learning (SSL) also held great promise, because it can learn robust high-level representations by training on pretext tasks before solving a supervised downstream task. Most current self-supervised models are based on contrastive learning. However, it is not straightforward to choose the pretext task to learn a good representation, and contrastive learning has been applied to medical images relatively little. To tackle this, a self-supervised framework with lesion-based contrastive learning was used for automated diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading.

- new longitudinal pretext task for classification
- Rivail et al.: LSSL Siamese model predicting time interval between two consecutive retinal OCT acquisitions -> captures disease progression
- Zhao et al.: LSSL auto-encoder on two consecutive scans; reconstruction term + time alignment term pushing latent topology along longitudinal changes
- later extension: dynamic graph per training batch -> neighborhood in latent space per subject; connects nearby subjects, aligns progression directions (smooth trajectory field)
- our aim: LSSL to predict change from no DR/mild NPDR (grade 0 or 1) to more severe DR (grade \geq 2) over two consecutive follow-ups
- three methods using current and prior examinations; comprehensive comparison on OPHDIAT dataset
- first work assessing early DR severity changes between consecutive images with SSL in longitudinal context

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The International Diabetes Federation expects that the number of people affected by diabetes will reach 700 million by 2045. Diabetic retinopathy (DR) affects more than one-third of this population and it is the leading cause of vision loss worldwide. DR happens when high blood sugar levels damage the retinal blood vessels, which causes swelling and leakage. In fundus retina images the lesions appear as leaking blood and fluids. Red lesions and bright lesions are the types of lesions that are commonly identified during DR screening. If DR is detected at an early stage, the incidence of blindness can be reduced. In clinical routine, color fundus photographs (CFP) are used to identify morphological changes of the retina, by looking at the presence of retinal lesions like microaneurysms, hemorrhages, and soft or hard exudates. The international clinical DR severity scale has five levels: no apparent DR, mild non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR), moderate NPDR, severe NPDR, and proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), which are labeled as grades 0, 1, 2, 3 (shown in Fig. 1) and 4. NPDR (grades 1, 2, 3) is the early-to-middle stage of DR, and it is a progressive microvascular disease with small vessel damages and occlusions. PDR (grade 4) is the period of potential visual loss, which is often caused by a massive hemorrhage. Identifying DR early and treating it adequately, especially in the mild to moderate stage of NPDR, may slow down the progression of DR and so prevent diabetes-related visual impairments and blindness.

In the past years deep learning has been very successful in medical image analysis. Many supervised learning techniques based on convolutional neural networks have been proposed for the automated DR grading task. But these approaches rarely make use of longitudinal information. In this direction, Yan et al. proposed to use a Siamese network with different pre-training and fusion schemes to detect the early stage of DR with longitudinal pairs of CFP acquired from the same patient. Self-supervised learning (SSL) also held great promise, because it can learn robust high-level representations by training on pretext tasks before solving a supervised downstream task. Most current self-supervised models are based on contrastive learning. However, it is not straightforward to choose the pretext task to learn a good representation, and contrastive learning has been applied to medical images relatively little. To tackle this, a self-supervised framework with lesion-based contrastive learning was used for automated diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading.

More recently a new pretext task appeared for classification in a longitudinal context. Rivail et al. proposed a longitudinal self-supervised learning Siamese model which is trained to predict the time interval between two consecutive longitudinal retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT) acquisitions, and in this way it captures the disease progression. Zhao et al. proposed an auto-encoder called LSSL that takes two consecutive longitudinal scans as inputs. In addition to the classic reconstruction term they added a time alignment term, which forces the topology of the latent space to change in the direction of the longitudinal changes. An extension of this principle was given in later work. To get a smooth trajectory field, a dynamic graph was computed in each training batch to define a neighborhood in the latent space for each subject. The graph connects nearby subjects and enforces their progression directions to be maximally aligned.

In this regard, our aim is to use LSSL approaches to capture the disease progression in order to predict the change between no DR/mild NPDR (grade 0 or 1) and more severe DR (grade \geq 2) over two consecutive follow-ups. For this we explore three methods that incorporate the current and the prior examinations. Then we do a comprehensive evaluation comparing these pipelines on the OPHDIAT dataset. As far as we know, this work is the first one to automatically assess early DR severity changes between consecutive images using self-supervised learning applied in a longitudinal context.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
According to the International Diabetes Federation, the number of people affected by diabetes is expected to reach 700 million by 2045 [1]. Diabetic retinopathy (DR) affects over one-third of this population and is the leading cause of vision loss worldwide [2]. It occurs when the retinal blood vessels are damaged by high blood sugar levels, causing swelling and leakage. In fundus retina images, lesions appear as leaking blood and fluids; red and bright lesions are the types commonly identified during DR screening. The incidence of blindness can be reduced if DR is detected at an early stage. In clinical routine, color fundus photographs (CFP) are employed to identify morphological changes of the retina by examining the presence of retinal lesions such as microaneurysms, hemorrhages, and soft or hard exudates. The international clinical DR severity scale includes no apparent DR, mild non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR), moderate NPDR, severe NPDR, and proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), labeled as grades 0, 1, 2, 3 (illustrated in Fig. 1) and 4. NPDR (grades 1, 2, 3) corresponds to the early-to-middle stage of DR and is a progressive microvascular disease characterized by small vessel damages and occlusions. PDR (grade 4) corresponds to the period of potential visual loss, often due to a massive hemorrhage. Early identification and adequate treatment, particularly in the mild to moderate stage of NPDR, may slow the progression of DR and consequently prevent diabetes-related visual impairments and blindness.

In the past years, deep learning has achieved great success in medical image analysis, and many supervised learning techniques based on convolutional neural networks have been proposed for the automated DR grading task [3,4,5]. Nevertheless, these approaches rarely take advantage of longitudinal information. In this direction, Yan et al. [6] proposed to exploit a Siamese network with different pre-training and fusion schemes to detect the early stage of DR using longitudinal pairs of CFP acquired from the same patient. Further, self-supervised learning (SSL) holds great promise, as it can learn robust high-level representations by training on pretext tasks [7] before solving a supervised downstream task. Current self-supervised models are largely based on contrastive learning [8,9]. However, choosing the pretext task to learn a good representation is not straightforward, and the application of contrastive learning to medical images remains relatively limited. To tackle this, a self-supervised framework using lesion-based contrastive learning was employed for automated diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading [10].

More recently, a new pretext task has appeared for classification purposes in a longitudinal context. Rivail et al. [12] proposed a longitudinal self-supervised learning Siamese model trained to predict the time interval between two consecutive longitudinal retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT) acquisitions, thus capturing the disease progression. Zhao et al. [13] proposed an auto-encoder named LSSL that takes two consecutive longitudinal scans as inputs, adding to the classic reconstruction term a time alignment term that forces the topology of the latent space to change in the direction of longitudinal changes. An extension of this principle was provided in [14]: to reach a smooth trajectory field, a dynamic graph was computed in each training batch to define a neighborhood in the latent space for each subject. The graph connects nearby subjects and enforces their progression directions to be maximally aligned.

In this regard, we aim to use LSSL approaches to capture the disease progression in order to predict the change between no DR/mild NPDR (grade 0 or 1) and more severe DR (grade \geq 2) through two consecutive follow-ups. To this end, we explore three methods incorporating current and prior examinations, and we conduct a comprehensive evaluation comparing these pipelines on the OPHDIAT dataset [11]. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to automatically assess early DR severity changes between consecutive images using self-supervised learning applied in a longitudinal context.
